use: What a contract leaves unsaid is given by the kernel rules, read this way. An operator is a computed node, or a module's few nodes, on a graph. Its inputs are distinct nodes: one given twice is refused when the operator is built. It runs at most once per wave, on each input's arrays in order (R-wave, R-invocation). It is given of a wave what R-invalidation leaves: DATA an input sent before its own INVALIDATE in the same wave is gone, so the operator does not count it, collect it, send it on or give it to a callback, though it would have in a wave of its own. How the inputs of one wave combine is each contract's to say; where a contract says nothing, they are taken in declared order. Its snapshot is the last array it sent that carried DATA (R-subscription). An input's effective INVALIDATE retracts the operator's retained output and keeps its private state; it does not undo occurrences already delivered (R-invalidation). When one input's INVALIDATE and another input's DATA come in one wave, the retraction goes out first and the DATA after it, whatever their order in the wave. An input's ERROR ends the operator with that ERROR, also when another input completes in that wave: it does not process that wave's DATA or call a callback for it, and what it had pending is not sent, unless its contract says it ends itself first. It completes once every input has ended (R-terminals). When its input's COMPLETE ends it in a wave in which it also sends DATA, DATA it sends because the input completed goes in the COMPLETE's array, and after DATA it would have sent anyway the COMPLETE is an array of its own. An operator that ends itself at a DATA says in its own contract where its COMPLETE goes. A throw from a callback is the operator's ERROR (R-failure). So is a callback's result that the operator must send as DATA and that is not a value (R-messages). Whether a predicate's result holds, and whether two values are the same when no equality is given, is each language's to say. A timer's firing is a new wave: no timer holds a wave open (R-wave). Progress is private state, which lasts for one activation: an operator that deactivates without having ended forgets it, and at its next activation runs on its inputs' snapshots as at its first (R-lifetime). A checkpoint saves it, and a restored operator does not take an unchanged input for a new occurrence (R-checkpoint). An operator given a callback can be captured only when the callback comes with a recipe, a reference and a configuration that can be saved, and it can be restored only where the restoring host's registry holds that reference; a package supplies the recipes of its built-in operators (R-node, R-checkpoint).
rationale: The other contracts state only what differs from this reading, so each stays short. DS-20 asks that a reader can predict a trace from the short contracts and common principles. Declared order for the inputs of one wave is DS-20's tie-breaker for merge and race, and the note of 2026-11-08 in reference/kernel/sugar.mjs gives it for the combinators as agreed with the user, whose words of that day are not recorded; the user confirmed it as the default for every operator on 2026-11-21 ("都按推荐"), after the independent review by Codex found the general sentence without recorded words. No kernel rule states it. The sentence on one activation is DS-20's: lifetime closure drops private state, and on later activation an unended computed node runs on dependency snapshots. Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: where a COMPLETE goes when DATA is sent in its wave, one sentence for every operator in place of one per contract; no kernel rule says it of a node that is not quiet. The sentence on DATA before an INVALIDATE is R-invalidation's, stated here because a contract's 'every DATA' would otherwise say more than an operator is given. Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: truth and default equality are each language's, since one rule for all would impose one language's on the others. That an ERROR ends an operator also in the wave of another input's COMPLETE the user decided that day for sample and buffer; stating it here for every operator was this item's, which the whole-branch review of 2026-11-21 pointed out, and the user confirmed it for every operator that day ("确认写入"). Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: an operator's inputs are distinct, where a repeated one had made a race end with a kernel refusal and a concat wait on itself; a result that is not a value is an ERROR for every operator that must send it, as for scan and reduce; and a retraction goes out before another input's DATA of the same wave, which the reference kernel does for every operator and no kernel rule states (graphrefly:B148). Decided by the user on 2026-11-21 ("都按推荐"), on this item's recommendation after the verification re-run: an operator that an input's ERROR ends calls no callback for that wave's DATA, which the reference did for every operator and only O-tap said; takeWhile and first, whose contracts have them read that DATA to see whether they end first, call their predicate for it. The sentence on capture and restore was reworded on 2026-11-21 after the same review: a recipe whose reference no registry holds is captured and is refused at the restore, as R-checkpoint and DS-20 say, where the sentence had made registration a condition of capture.

rationale: graphrefly:D829, decided by the user on 2026-11-24 ("都按建议办", and "按草稿写" to the wording): the sentence on a callback's result that is not a node is new (graphrefly:B151). The contracts had said what a throw of a project or of a handler does and nothing of such a result; the reference ended the operator by an accidental error, but for a switchMap that selected no inner, which went on for null. Everything else is O-common@1's, whose rationale stands.

use: derived(f) computes f from the latest value of every dependency and sends the result. It computes only while every dependency has a value, and sends one result per run in which a dependency delivered DATA. It reads values, not occurrences: a value in the middle of an array is not computed on. A dependency that has ended keeps its value. It is the one latest-value combinator; there is no combine alias.
rationale: DS-20: state management gets a state and derived pair; map sees every occurrence, derived computes from latest values and covers latest-state combination without another public alias. Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: derived computes only while every dependency has a value, at its first run and at every later one. graphrefly:D797 (9) had left that gate to each language; under graphrefly:D813 the contract states it for all, which does not supersede D797 (9) (graphrefly:D816 (4)).

use: map(f) sends f(v) for every DATA v of its source, in order, one output array for each input array.
filter(p) sends the DATA for which p holds, in order, each in the array it came in. An array left with no DATA is not sent.

tap(f) calls f(v) once for every DATA it is given, in order, and sends that DATA on in the arrays it came in; what f returns is not read. In the wave of its source's ERROR it is given no DATA, so f is not called; nor is f called for an INVALIDATE or a terminal. A throw from f ends the branch with ERROR. There is no onFirstData.
rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: f is called for the DATA tap sends on, so it is not called for DATA in the wave of the source's ERROR, which no operator under the default policy is given. Reworded after the third review: 'the DATA it sends' did not hold when f throws later in the same run, since what the run had passed to f is then not sent (graphrefly:B148).

use: scan(f, seed) keeps an accumulator that starts at seed and sends f(accumulator, v) for every DATA v, each intermediate in the array its input came in. The seed itself is not sent. The seed is required: there is no form without one. f returns the next accumulator and does not change the one it is given, nor the seed; scan does not guard against an f that does. A result of f that is not a value ends scan with ERROR in that wave.

exceptions.statement: A source INVALIDATE retracts the output and keeps the accumulator. The reducer is not called and the accumulator is not sent; the next DATA goes on from it.

rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-20 ("必须给 seed"): scan and reduce require a seed. This item's recommendation, which the user took on 2026-11-20, gave these reasons: scan and reduce differ in when they send, not in having a seed; a required seed gives reduce its result for an empty source, keeps one shape of private state for a checkpoint, and fixes the accumulator's type in a typed language; a form without a seed can be added later without changing this one. Also decided by the user that day, on this item's recommendations: f must not change the accumulator it is given, where the other course, a copy of the seed at each activation, would keep the seed and still let values already sent change within a wave; and a result that is not a value is an ERROR, which scan could not send anyway.

use: reduce(f, seed) accumulates as scan does, under the same terms for f and the seed, and sends nothing until its source completes normally; then it sends the result and COMPLETE in one array. An empty source gives the seed. A result of f that is not a value ends reduce with ERROR in the wave f returned it, though reduce would not have sent it then.

exceptions.statement: A source ERROR ends reduce with that ERROR and the pending result is not sent.
The accumulator is kept across a source INVALIDATE; f is not called and nothing is sent. A source that completes right after it gives what was accumulated before.

rationale: The seed is required for the reasons given at O-scan (the user, 2026-11-20). Decided by the user the same day, on this item's recommendation: a result of f that is not a value ends reduce in that wave, as it ends scan, where reduce had gone on and failed only if the last result was not a value.

use: distinctUntilChanged(equal?) sends a DATA only when it differs from the last DATA it sent, each in the array it came in; an array left with none is not sent. The first DATA passes. Two values are the same when equal(last sent, candidate) holds or, without equal, by the language's documented equality.

exceptions.statement: A source INVALIDATE retracts the output and clears what is compared against, so the next DATA passes even when it equals the retracted value, also when it follows the INVALIDATE in the same wave.

A restored distinctUntilChanged keeps what it compares against together with its output, also when its source holds no value at its first activation: what it compares against is the last value of its output, and R-checkpoint keeps the output. Without equal, whether a value read back from a checkpoint is the same as the one that was saved is the language's equality to say: where that equality is identity, a list or a record is not, and one value the original would have dropped passes after a restore; in such a language a structured value needs an equal to be compared across a restore.

rationale: DS-20: keeping the baseline could leave a downstream snapshot empty for good while valid equal values keep arriving. Decided by the user on 2026-11-20 ("都按现在的写法"), on this item's reading: the equality is given the last sent value first and the candidate second. Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: a restored distinctUntilChanged keeps its baseline with its output, where a restored sample discards a pending value it never sent. Decided by the user on 2026-11-21 ("都按推荐"), on this item's recommendation after the whole-branch review: the default equality stays each language's, and the contract says what follows for a structured value across a checkpoint, which a fuzzed restore had shown on the reference (identity against a saved copy). Reworded on 2026-11-21 after the independent review by Codex, which showed by a probe that the sentence could be read to predict something the reference and the traces do not give; no behavior changed.

use: pairwise sends [previous, current] for every DATA from the second on. A pair may span two arrays or two waves, and goes out in the array of its second value. A DATA read while there is no previous value only becomes the previous one: the first DATA of every activation but a restored one, whose previous value is saved.

exceptions.statement: A source INVALIDATE retracts the output and keeps the previous value: A, INVALIDATE, B still gives the pair [A, B].

use: take(n) sends the first n DATA and completes in the array of the nth; what its source sends after the nth is not sent. n is a nonnegative integer; take(0) completes on activation, whatever its source holds or has ended with.

exceptions.statement: The branch ends at the nth DATA: an ERROR that follows that DATA, in the same wave or in the snapshot take activates on, is not sent, since it reaches a branch that has ended. To see whether it ends first, take reads the DATA of a wave that carries an ERROR.

A source INVALIDATE retracts the retained output and leaves the count already seen: only DATA is counted, an open branch goes on with the next DATA, and a branch that has ended stays ended with its snapshot.

rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-20 ("都按现在的写法"), on this item's reading: an ERROR that follows the nth DATA in the same wave is not sent, as takeUntil's notifier DATA ends its branch whatever ERROR the wave carries. Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: the ERROR is not sent also when DATA and ERROR come together in the snapshot take activates on, as an operator that had been active would have ended at the DATA; and take(0) completes on activation whatever its source holds, so the earlier 'reads nothing' is gone, the kernel activating the source all the same.

use: skip(n) drops the first n DATA and sends the rest, each in the array it came in; an array left with none is not sent. n is a nonnegative integer; skip(0) passes everything.

exceptions.statement: A source INVALIDATE retracts the retained output and leaves the count already seen: only DATA is counted.

use: takeWhile(p) sends DATA while p holds and completes at the first DATA for which it does not, without sending that one: the COMPLETE goes in the array takeWhile was sending then, or alone when that array holds nothing yet. p is not called again.

exceptions.statement: The branch ends at the DATA for which p does not hold: an ERROR that follows that DATA, in the same wave or in the snapshot takeWhile activates on, is not sent, since it reaches a branch that has ended. To see whether it ends first, takeWhile reads the DATA of a wave that carries an ERROR, and calls p for it.
A source INVALIDATE retracts the retained output and calls no predicate. An open branch goes on with the next DATA; a branch the predicate has ended stays ended with its snapshot.

rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-20 ("都按现在的写法"), on this item's reading: the COMPLETE goes in the array takeWhile was sending when the predicate failed, as take's goes in the array of the nth, and an ERROR that follows that DATA in the same wave is not sent. Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: the ERROR is not sent also when DATA and ERROR come together in the snapshot takeWhile activates on. That p is called for the DATA of a wave that carries an ERROR is what reading it means; it is written out since O-common says no callback is called for such DATA (the user, 2026-11-21).

use: first(p?) sends the first DATA, or the first for which p holds, and completes in the same array; p is not called again. When the source completes without one, first completes without DATA. There is no find and no elementAt.

exceptions.statement: The branch ends at the DATA it sends: an ERROR that follows that DATA, in the same wave or in the snapshot first activates on, is not sent, since it reaches a branch that has ended. To see whether it ends first, first reads the DATA of a wave that carries an ERROR, and calls p for it.
A source INVALIDATE calls no predicate and leaves an open branch open; a branch that has matched stays ended with its snapshot.

rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-20 ("都按现在的写法"), on this item's reading: an ERROR that follows the matching DATA in the same wave is not sent. Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: the ERROR is not sent also when DATA and ERROR come together in the snapshot first activates on. That p is called for the DATA of a wave that carries an ERROR is what reading it means; it is written out since O-common says no callback is called for such DATA (the user, 2026-11-21).

use: last(p?) sends the last DATA, or the last for which p held, with COMPLETE in one array when its source completes normally. An empty source, or one in which nothing matched, completes without DATA. p is called for every DATA last is given, as it comes.

exceptions.statement: A source ERROR ends last with that ERROR and the candidate is not sent.
The candidate is kept across a source INVALIDATE: DATA(A), INVALIDATE, COMPLETE in separate waves gives [DATA(A), COMPLETE]. The operator answers which occurrence last matched during the lifetime.

rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-21 ("确认写入"), on this item's reading, which the whole-branch review had found without a source: p is called for every DATA as it comes, and not when the source completes. DS-20 says only that last can take a predicate and flushes on normal completion. It decides in which wave a throw from p ends last.

use: merge sends every input's arrays as they came; within one wave, inputs go in declared order. Its snapshot is the last array it sent that carried DATA, not the latest value among its inputs. It completes when every input has completed, and any input's ERROR ends it.

exceptions.statement: Any input's effective INVALIDATE retracts the output, also when another input supplied it.

rationale: The snapshot sentence and the invalidation sentence were added after the independent review (Q3, 2026-11-18); both follow from R-subscription and R-invalidation and are not new choices. Reworded on 2026-11-21 after the independent review by Codex, which showed by a probe that the sentence could be read to predict something the reference and the traces do not give; no behavior changed.

use: withLatestFrom(primary, ...secondaries) sends, for each DATA of the primary, the list of that value followed by the latest value of each secondary in declared order, one output array for each primary array. A primary occurrence is dropped while any secondary has no value. A secondary's occurrence alone sends nothing. A value the primary holds when withLatestFrom activates is an occurrence as any other: it is sent with the secondaries' latest values, at every activation but a restored one's first, where a primary value withLatestFrom had already received is not an occurrence again.

exceptions.statement: When a secondary delivers in the wave of a primary occurrence, the pair holds the secondary's final value for that wave.
The primary's COMPLETE ends the branch. A secondary that completed keeps its latest value. Any input's ERROR ends the branch.

An INVALIDATE of either kind of input retracts the output. A secondary's INVALIDATE also clears that secondary's latest value, so primary occurrences are dropped until it delivers again. A primary's INVALIDATE leaves the secondaries' latest values.

rationale: The pair of the primary's value and the secondary's latest is the combinators' shape that the note of 2026-11-08 in reference/kernel/sugar.mjs gives as agreed with the user, whose words of that day are not recorded; with several secondaries the list goes on in declared order. Decided by the user on 2026-11-21 ("都按推荐"), on this item's recommendation after the whole-branch review: the primary's value at activation is sent, where a sample's clock value at activation is not a tick. The primary's value is data that goes into the output; a clock's value is a signal and is not read. DS-20 calls the primary a primary clock, so the difference is stated. The review of the fix round found that "at every activation" said more than O-common allows a restored operator; the exception is O-common's and R-checkpoint's, written out as O-pairwise writes its own.

use: zip queues each input's DATA by position and sends, in one array, every tuple that can be formed in a run, each the list of one item from every input in declared order. It has no capacity and drops nothing. It ends when an input that has completed has no queued item left, and its COMPLETE goes in the array of that run's tuples.

exceptions.statement: What several inputs deliver in one wave is queued together, and the tuples it forms go out in that wave. zip ends itself at the tuple that leaves an input that has completed with nothing queued: an ERROR of that wave, or of the snapshot zip activates on, is then not sent, whichever input it is of, since it reaches a zip that has ended. To see whether it ends first, zip reads the DATA of a wave that carries an ERROR.

It ends when any input has completed with nothing queued, also while another still has items. DATA that comes with an input's COMPLETE is queued first. An input that has ended with ERROR does not end zip in that way: its ERROR ends zip without that run's tuples, unless one of them ended zip first.
An input's INVALIDATE retracts the output and keeps the unmatched queues, that input's own included.

rationale: That the COMPLETE shares the array of the run's tuples is graphrefly:D797 (9), which differs from O-common's sentence for other operators. Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: an ERROR that follows the DATA that ends zip is not sent, as for take, takeWhile, first and takeUntil. Decided by the user on 2026-11-21 ("都按推荐"), on this item's recommendation after the review of the fix round: the input whose empty queue ends zip is one that completed normally, where DS-20's 'ended' could be read to count an ERROR; an input that ended with ERROR ends zip with that ERROR and the tuple of that run is not sent, as the reference did; and the same holds in the snapshot zip activates on, a clause the round before had added without a decision.

use: zip queues each input's DATA by position and sends, in one array, every tuple that can be formed in a run, each the list of one item from every input in declared order. It has no capacity and drops nothing. It ends when an input that has completed has no queued item left, and its COMPLETE goes in the array of that run's tuples.

exceptions.statement: What several inputs deliver in one wave is queued together, and the tuples it forms go out in that wave. zip ends itself at the tuple that leaves an input that has completed with nothing queued: an ERROR of that wave, or of the snapshot zip activates on, is then not sent, whichever input it is of, since it reaches a zip that has ended. To see whether it ends first, zip reads the DATA of a wave that carries an ERROR.

It ends when any input has completed with nothing queued, also while another still has items. DATA that comes with an input's COMPLETE is queued first. An input that has ended with ERROR does not end zip in that way: its ERROR ends zip without that run's tuples, unless one of them ended zip first. An input replaced by a new instance (R-subscription) is no longer counted as completed; what zip queued from the old instance stays.
An input's INVALIDATE retracts the output and keeps the unmatched queues, that input's own included.

rationale: graphrefly:D820, decided by the user on 2026-11-23 ("按草稿写"): since graphrefly:D819 a function is told that an input was replaced by a new instance, and zip, the one operator of the set that records an input's COMPLETE, ended while the new instance was open (graphrefly:B148's eleventh point). It drops nothing, so its queue stays. Everything else is O-zip@1's, whose rationale stands.

use: concat follows one source at a time, in the order given, and subscribes to the next only when the current one completes; when the last one completes, concat completes. It subscribes by making the next source its one dependency (R-request-order), so what that source holds arrives as a wave of its own. A source it comes to later gives its ordinary snapshot; what that source sent before is not replayed, and one that has already completed is passed in turn. Every source exists when concat is built.

exceptions.statement: The current source's INVALIDATE retracts the output. Only the current source's COMPLETE subscribes the next.
Only the current source's terminal reaches concat: a later source may complete before its turn without effect, and the current source's ERROR ends concat.

rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-20, on this item's recommendation: every source exists when concat is built, where a missing one had only failed at its turn, losing that wave's DATA.

use: race selects the first input to deliver DATA or a terminal, then releases the others and follows the one selected: its arrays, and its terminal.

exceptions.statement: When several inputs are eligible in one wave, the first in declared order is selected. What the others deliver in that wave, an ERROR included, is not sent.

Before the selection no INVALIDATE retracts anything, since race has sent nothing. After it only the selected input's INVALIDATE retracts the output, also while the others are still being released, and the selection stands. An input that was invalidated before race activated and holds no DATA when it does cannot be selected for a value, so another input can win; if it has ended, its terminal makes it eligible as any input's does, and among several that are eligible the first in declared order is selected.
An input that lost does not end race, whatever it ends with. An input that has only ended, with no value, can be selected.

rationale: Reworded on 2026-11-21 after the independent review by Codex, which showed by a probe that the sentence could be read to predict something the reference and the traces do not give; no behavior changed. Reworded again that day after Codex re-checked the fixes: the first rewording had itself said too much, which a probe showed.

use: sample(source, clock) sends the source's pending value at a clock DATA. A value is sent once: further ticks, in the same wave or later, send nothing until the source delivers again. What the clock delivers in the run of sample's activation is not a tick, whatever the clock held or sent then; clock DATA in any later wave is. A clock that had ended with ERROR when sample activates ends it, as O-common says of an input's ERROR: an ERROR is a terminal, not a tick.

exceptions.statement: The wave's source DATA is taken before the clock's: a source that sends [1, 2] in the wave of one tick gives 2. A tick in the wave of the source's COMPLETE takes the pending value, which is sent before the COMPLETE.
The source's COMPLETE ends sample, and a pending value that no tick of that wave took is not sent. The clock's COMPLETE alone does not end sampling.

A source INVALIDATE retracts the output and discards the pending value, so a tick sends nothing until the source delivers again. A clock INVALIDATE retracts nothing and takes no tick: the output and the pending value stay, also in a wave that ends sample with an ERROR. A clock DATA that follows it in the wave still samples.

At a restored sample's first activation, as at any activation, what the clock holds is not a tick, also when it differs from what sample had received. The saved state stands: the pending value is kept, and a source value sample had already received is not read again. A source value that changed is the new pending value. When the source holds no value then, the pending value is discarded; the output is kept, as R-checkpoint keeps a restored node's own value.

rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-20: the source's COMPLETE ends sample; the clock's value at activation is not a tick, by the run and not by where the value came from; a tick in the wave of the source's COMPLETE still samples; what the clock holds at a restored sample's first activation is not a tick either, and a restored sample discards a pending value whose source was invalidated meanwhile. This item's recommendation, which the user took on 2026-11-20, gave these reasons: a clock is often a state that keeps the value of its last use, and taking that for a tick would fire every sample built over it later; and a restore compares values, so it could not see a tick of an equal value, which would make a tick while saved count only sometimes. Also decided by the user that day, on this item's recommendations: a clock INVALIDATE never retracts the output, also in the wave of an ERROR, where the default ERROR policy would have retracted it; and where the COMPLETE goes is O-common's to say, the user having decided only that the value goes first. Decided by the user on 2026-11-21 ("都按推荐"), on this item's recommendation after the review of the fix round: a clock that had ended with ERROR when sample activates ends it, as the reference did; what is not a tick in the run of activation is the clock's DATA. Reworded on 2026-11-21 after the independent review by Codex, which showed by a probe that the sentence could be read to predict something the reference and the traces do not give; no behavior changed.

use: takeUntil(source, notifier) sends the source's arrays, each as it came, until the notifier delivers DATA, and then completes. What the notifier delivers in the run of takeUntil's activation does not stop it, whatever the notifier held or sent then; notifier DATA in any later wave does. A notifier that had ended with ERROR when takeUntil activates ends it, as O-common says of an input's ERROR: only the notifier's DATA is what does not stop the branch then. It is not resource cancellation, which an AbortSignal handles.

exceptions.statement: A notifier DATA in a wave completes the branch. Neither the source's DATA of that wave nor any ERROR in it, the source's or the notifier's own, is sent.
The source's COMPLETE ends the branch at once, also while the notifier is open, and is sent as an array of its own after that wave's source arrays. The notifier's COMPLETE alone does nothing.

A source INVALIDATE retracts the output, and an open branch keeps listening to both inputs; in the wave that stops the branch it retracts the output before the COMPLETE. A notifier INVALIDATE retracts nothing and stops nothing: by itself it leaves the branch open and its output in place, also in a wave in which an ERROR ends the branch. Only notifier DATA stops it. A branch that has ended stays ended.

At a restored takeUntil's first activation, as at any activation, what the notifier holds does not stop it, also when it differs from what takeUntil had received. The output it had sent is kept, also when the source holds no value then, as R-checkpoint keeps a restored node's own value.

rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-20: the source's COMPLETE ends the branch at once and goes out as an array of its own, as a map's does; the notifier's value at activation does not stop it, by the run and not by where the value came from; a notifier DATA completes the branch whatever ERROR the wave carries, the source's or the notifier's own; what the notifier holds at a restored takeUntil's first activation does not stop it either. This item's recommendation, which the user took on 2026-11-20, gave these reasons: the notifier can only stop the branch early, so a source that has ended leaves nothing to wait for; a notifier is often a state that keeps the value of its last use; a switch in switchMap already drops the superseded inner's ERROR of the switching wave (Q2), which is the same case; and the notifier's own ERROR follows its DATA, so it reaches a branch that has ended, as it would in a later wave. That the source's arrays pass each as it came is graphrefly:D797 (9)'s rule for an occurrence combinator. Decided by the user on 2026-11-21 ("都按推荐"), on this item's recommendation after the review of the fix round: a notifier that had ended with ERROR when takeUntil activates ends it, as the reference did. Reworded on 2026-11-21 after the independent review by Codex, which showed by a probe that the sentence could be read to predict something the reference and the traces do not give; no behavior changed. Reworded again that day after Codex re-checked the fixes: the first rewording had itself said too much, which a probe showed.

use: buffer(source, flush) collects the source's DATA payloads, dropping only how they were grouped into arrays, and at a flush DATA sends what it collected as one DATA. An empty batch is not sent. DATA([1,2]) then DATA(3) gives [[1,2],3]; three scalar occurrences give [1,2,3]. What the flush input delivers in the run of buffer's activation is not a flush, whatever it held or sent then; its DATA in any later wave is. A flush input that had ended with ERROR when buffer activates ends it, as O-common says of an input's ERROR: an ERROR is a terminal, not a flush.

exceptions.statement: The wave's source DATA is taken before the flush: a source that sends [1, 2] in the wave of one flush gives the batch [1, 2]. A flush in the wave of the source's COMPLETE sends what was collected as an array of its own, before the COMPLETE.

The source's normal COMPLETE sends a nonempty tail in the terminal's array, and with nothing collected the COMPLETE alone. An ERROR of either input drops the tail. The flush input's COMPLETE alone does not end collection.

A source INVALIDATE retracts the output and keeps the collected payloads, also in the wave of a flush or of the source's COMPLETE: A, INVALIDATE, B may still give the batch [A, B]. A flush INVALIDATE retracts nothing: the last batch stays the output, also in a wave that ends buffer with an ERROR, and the pending batch waits for a flush DATA or the source's normal COMPLETE.

At a restored buffer's first activation, as at any activation, what the flush input holds is not a flush, also when it differs from what buffer had received. The saved state stands: the collected payloads are kept, and a source value buffer had already received is not collected again.

rationale: DS-20: buffer promises a batch of observed occurrences, so it keeps payloads a pausable would discard. Wave and array grouping are history's to keep (R-history). Decided by the user on 2026-11-20: the flush input's value at activation is not a flush, by the run and not by where the value came from, at a restored buffer's first activation too. use: bufferCount(n) collects the source's DATA payloads, as buffer does, and sends each n of them as one DATA. n is a positive integer and batches do not overlap.

exceptions.statement: Batches formed in one run are sent each as its own array, in order, so the snapshot is always one batch.
The source's normal COMPLETE sends a nonempty tail in the terminal's array; with no tail the COMPLETE is an array of its own, after that run's batches. A source ERROR drops the tail.
A source INVALIDATE retracts the output and keeps the collected payloads.

rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-20: each batch is its own array. This item's recommendation, which the user took on 2026-11-20, gave the reason that a new subscriber then sees the latest batch, as it does when values arrive one in a wave, whether or not an upstream happened to write several values in one wave. use: switchMap(project) follows the inner Node that project returns for the latest outer value, releasing the one before it, and sends the selected inner's DATA. After the outer's COMPLETE it ends when the selected inner ends, or at once when none is selected. An inner's ERROR, the outer's ERROR or a throw from project ends the branch with ERROR.

exceptions.statement: Only the last outer value of a wave is projected. The new selection is applied first: DATA and ERROR that the superseded inner delivers in the switching wave are not sent. Its INVALIDATE in that wave still retracts the output. An outer value that projects to the definition already attached supersedes nothing.

An outer INVALIDATE retracts the output, releases the selected inner and ignores what that selection delivers afterwards. What the released inner delivers in that wave is not sent either. The selected inner's INVALIDATE retracts the output and the inner stays attached. An inner already detached has no say over the output.

A checkpoint keeps the selected inner's identity and recipe and whether the outer completed. The inner is built again without calling project, and neither an unchanged saved outer value nor an inner snapshot already sent is a new occurrence. A restored switchMap whose outer no longer holds a value had its outer invalidated while the graph was saved, and releases its selected inner, as it would have. The output is kept, as R-checkpoint keeps a restored node's own value.

use: mergeMap(project, capacity?) projects every outer value to an inner Node and sends the DATA of every inner it holds. An outer value that projects to a definition it already holds adds no inner and takes no slot. capacity is a positive integer; without one there is no bound. Outer values beyond the capacity wait in order, unprojected, and are projected only when admitted. After the outer's COMPLETE it ends when the accepted work is done. An inner's ERROR, the outer's ERROR or a throw from project ends the branch with ERROR.

exceptions.statement: In a run it first sends the DATA of the inners it already holds and frees the slots of inners that ended, then admits outer values in order.

An outer INVALIDATE retracts the output; accepted inners keep running and waiting outer values stay in order. An attached inner's INVALIDATE retracts the output, also when another inner supplied it, and the inner keeps its slot; a new subscriber sees no value until fresh DATA arrives.

A checkpoint keeps the accepted inners' identities and recipes, the waiting outer values in order and whether the outer completed. Accepted inners are built again without calling project, and neither an unchanged saved outer value nor an inner snapshot already sent is a new occurrence.

use: catchError(handler) follows its source; on the source's ERROR it calls handler(error) once and follows the Node the handler returns, which gives its ordinary snapshot and terminal. DATA already sent stays sent, the DATA that came before the ERROR in the same array included. A normal COMPLETE passes without the handler. It switches at most once; a second fallback is a second catchError. There is no rescue.

exceptions.statement: A throw from the handler, or the replacement's ERROR, ends the branch with that new ERROR.

An INVALIDATE of the branch it follows retracts the output and changes no selection: the source's ERROR can still switch once after it, and on the replacement the selection stays. An INVALIDATE never calls or re-arms the handler. In a wave that carries an INVALIDATE and then a terminal, the INVALIDATE is applied first and then the terminal, once.
A catchError that had switched is restored on its replacement, and the handler is not called again.

A catchError that deactivated has forgotten that it switched (O-common), so its handler is called again at its next activation, and not at a restore. graphrefly-ts and graphrefly-rs have no catchError: their rescue turns the error into a value.

use: retry(policy) starts its inner again when it ends with an ERROR the policy retries, after the policy's delay. maxAttempts counts every attempt, the first included. DATA already sent stays sent. It is the restart owner and inner (R-restart).

While a retry waits the failed inner has ended; an INVALIDATE of a dependency the owner holds then retracts the output and keeps the pending attempt, its deadline and the budget. A new attempt reads the dependencies' values of that time. Only an ERROR schedules a retry.
A checkpoint keeps the attempts used. A retry that was waiting waits its delay again in full, for the same attempt.

With a retry policy an ERROR is retried as retry does, each round with a fresh attempt budget, counted apart from the rounds. DATA already sent stays sent. It is the restart owner and inner (R-restart).

exceptions.statement: An effective INVALIDATE of the active inner retracts the output and keeps the round. Only a normal COMPLETE advances the round.
A checkpoint keeps the rounds completed and the attempts used in the current round.

use: valve(source, control) sends the source's DATA while the control's value is true, and drops it otherwise. It starts closed and opens only on an explicit true. Reopening replays nothing, and it aborts no work in flight. There is no settle.

exceptions.statement: The control's final value of the wave decides for that wave's source DATA.
The source's COMPLETE ends the valve. The control's COMPLETE alone does not end it: a control that completed keeps its last value.

A source INVALIDATE retracts the retained output, also while the valve is closed. A control INVALIDATE alone leaves the control without a value, which closes the valve: the output sent before stays, and new DATA is dropped until the control is true again. In the wave of an ERROR a control INVALIDATE retracts nothing either.

rationale: DS-20: an explicit valve is preferable to a composition of three operators for common gating. Settle counts local runs and cannot establish convergence or elapsed silence by itself. Decided by the user on 2026-11-20: the source's COMPLETE ends the valve and the control's alone does not. This item's recommendation, which the user took on 2026-11-20, gave the reason that a control is often a long-lived state, and waiting for it would keep the valve from ever completing. use: A pausable holds the arrays that arrive while any lock is held and sends them, each as it arrived, when the last lock is released (R-pause).

exceptions.statement: A source INVALIDATE retracts the retained output, also while paused, and discards the arrays held before it, so a resume cannot send them. An INVALIDATE of the lock state leaves it without a list, which holds no lock: every held array is released in one wave, each as it arrived; with nothing held the output sent before stays. In a release wave that also carries a source INVALIDATE the held arrays older than it are discarded first, and only source DATA after it is released. In the wave of an ERROR an INVALIDATE of the lock state retracts nothing either.
The lock state's list after the wave decides for that wave's source arrays and for its terminal.

A restored pausable whose source no longer holds a value had its source invalidated while the graph was saved, and discards what it held, as it would have. The output is kept, as R-checkpoint keeps a restored node's own value.

The source's terminal passes at once and ends the pausable. While no lock is held the terminal goes out in the last array the pausable sends in that run, after its DATA, an ERROR's too, and alone when the run sends no DATA; while a lock is held the terminal goes alone and what was held is not sent. The lock state's COMPLETE alone does not end it: a lock state that completed keeps its list.

rationale: DS-20: only a present, nonempty list pauses. The cost is that invalidating a shared lock state removes every controller's lock at once; a single controller releases its own with resume(lock). The alternative considered was to hold until an explicit empty list arrives. Decided by the user on 2026-11-23 ("都按建议办"), on this item's recommendation. The completion exception follows R-pause and C-30 where O-common would have said otherwise: the source's terminal goes on in the array it came in, with its DATA, an ERROR's too. The lock state's COMPLETE alone does not end the pausable, as a valve's control's does not; its ERROR ends it, as O-common says of an input's ERROR, where the reference had passed over the lock state's terminal altogether. Decided by the user the same day ("都按建议改"), after a round of mutants written without sight of the traces: the sentence on the source's terminal first said that the array it came in goes on as it came, which a function cannot do, since it is not told which array a terminal came in; it now says what the reference does, the terminal in the last array of that run. The same-wave exception is new: the lock state's list after the wave decides, as DS-20 says of a control's final state for the wave. And an INVALIDATE of the lock state retracts nothing in the wave of an ERROR either, as the user decided of a valve's control. Decided by the user the same day ("都按建议办"), after a second such round. The sentence on the wave of an ERROR had said that it retracts nothing, which could be read of the pausable, and so of a source INVALIDATE too; it now names the lock state's INVALIDATE, and no behavior changed. The recovery exception is new, and follows O-sample's: until then a restored pausable sent, at its release, arrays its source had retracted while the graph was saved. What a restore cannot see stays as R-checkpoint says: an INVALIDATE followed by a write of another value is seen as the write, so what was held then stays and the new value follows it.

use: latestAsync(f) starts f(value, signal) for the latest input and sends its one result as a later wave. Only the newest job may publish: a newer input aborts the job before it, and a stale job's success or failure is ignored. f may give its result later, in the language's own deferred form.

exceptions.statement: Only the last input value of a wave starts a job.

After the source's COMPLETE the operator waits for the current job and then ends. With no current job it ends at once. The current job's failure ends the operator with an ERROR, its payload as R-failure gives a thrown value's.

A source INVALIDATE retracts the output, takes the current job's right to publish and aborts its signal; that job's later result or failure is ignored, also when no newer job started, when the job ignores cancellation, and before the first output. The operator stays active. DATA that follows the last INVALIDATE in the same wave starts one job, for its last value, with a fresh signal; without it the operator waits for input. PENDING or RESOLVED alone revokes no job.

The input a job is pending for is private state. At a restored operator's first activation it calls f again for that input, with a new signal. Whether that is fresh work or the same job found again is f's: a resumable f looks its job up by the input and must not submit a second external job by reattaching. A result already published stays the snapshot, and no job starts for an unchanged saved input. A restored latestAsync whose source no longer holds a value had its source invalidated while the graph was saved, and starts no job for the input it had pending. The output is kept, as R-checkpoint keeps a restored node's own value.

rationale: Decided by the user on 2026-11-24 (graphrefly:B147). The name stays latestAsync ("可以"): graphrefly-ts, graphrefly-py and graphrefly-rs each have the operation under another name and shape (switchMap over fromPromise; async_node over several dependencies with a runner; worker_derived on a worker pool), and none gives its callback a signal, revokes a job at an INVALIDATE or saves a pending input, which the maintainer's selection adds; the three are advised to ship it under this one name, each in its spelling, which is theirs to decide (graphrefly:D813), and several dependencies are a derived before it. To four proposals and seven readings ("都按建议办"): the use speaks of the language's own deferred form, where it had named JavaScript's Promise; the completion exception says what the current job's failure does, which the contract had not, the three runtimes giving three payloads; the recovery exception says what the operator does, calling f again for the pending input, and leaves to f whether that is fresh work or the same job, where it had spoken of two kinds of factory the operator cannot tell apart; and its last two sentences are new, and follow O-sample's, O-pause's, O-switchMap's and O-debounce's. The two sentences on a resumable factory that O-retry lost are not put back: a canonical trace holds what they meant, a restored retry of a latestAsync whose job was pending calling f again and using no attempt for it. Taken the same day as read, without a sentence: f is called in the run, for the wave's last value, so a throw of f is a throw of the function (R-failure); a result that is no deferred value is the result itself, and goes out as a later wave all the same; a result that is no value ends the operator with ERROR (O-common); the result that came after the source's COMPLETE is sent and the COMPLETE follows as an array of its own (O-common); a job that has published is done, and its signal is not aborted afterwards; a restored operator whose source changed while the graph was saved starts the new value's job alone; and what the source holds at activation starts a job, a deactivation aborting it and forgetting its input (O-common). Decided by the user on 2026-11-24 ("都按建议办", graphrefly:B151), both as the reference reads them and without a sentence. A value equal to the input a job is pending for is a newer input, which the use's 'a newer input' covers and a trace holds: whether two values are the same is each language's (O-common), and a distinctUntilChanged before the operator gives a dedupe. And a source INVALIDATE drops the input the job was pending for, which the invalidation exception gives in its effects, where O-common keeps private state: an input that was retracted has no right to publish.
